Day 2
The idea

From 70/20/10 to 50/30/20

On Day 1 you said your time splits 70% getting things done, 20% strategising and 10% developing the team. That split has to change.

JobNow and target
Getting things done70% now. Target 50% (or 40%)
Strategising20% now. Target 30%
Developing the team10% now. Target 20% (or 30%)
8
hours a week moved from doing the work to thinking ahead and growing people. That is twenty points of a 40 hour week.

Those hours do not appear by working harder. They come from six connected skills, and each part of this workbook covers one of them.

  1. 1
    Manage time so there is room to be strategic.
  2. 2
    Choose the essential. Decide what the freed hours are for.
  3. 3
    Delegate. Move work to the team, at the right level.
  4. 4
    Set KPIs and give feedback, so delegated work stays on track.
  5. 5
    Coach with GROW, so people need you less.
  6. 6
    Build a PDP. Turn development into a written plan.

The logic is one chain. If one link is missing, the split goes back to 70/20/10.

“Nearly half of their time is devoted to nonmanagerial work”McKinsey, on managers (Field, Hancock, Mugayar Baldocchi & Schaninger, 2023)

Part 1 · Time management

Time management

Making room to be strategic

Part 1 · Time management
The theory

Your week is cut into pieces

A manager’s week is not short of hours. It is cut into small pieces and filled with work other people could do. Strategic work needs long, quiet blocks, and those never appear on their own.

Time management for a manager is therefore three things: stop the leaks, remove low value work, and protect time for thinking.

What the research says

40%
Switching has a price. “even brief mental blocks created by shifting between tasks can cost as much as 40 percent of someone’s productive time”. This is an upper estimate, not an average.American Psychological Association (2006)
275
The typical worker is “interrupted every two minutes, 275 times per day”, and “57% of meetings are ad hoc calls without calendar invites.”Microsoft (2025)
41%
of knowledge workers’ time goes on activities that “could be handled competently by others.” After coaching, people “saved six hours of desk work and two hours of meeting time each week.”Birkinshaw & Cohen (2013)
Part 1 · Time management
The theory · Tool 1

Drop, Delegate, Redesign

Run every recurring task and meeting through three questions, in this order.

1. Drop“What would happen if I just dropped it completely?” If the honest answer is “nothing much”, it goes.
2. Delegate“Am I the only person who could do this task?” Part 3 covers how to hand it over properly.
3. Redesign“How could this task get completed if I only had half the time?” A status meeting becomes a written update. A recurring report becomes a dashboard.

The order matters. Dropping is cheapest, so it comes first. Many managers start with redesign and end up doing unnecessary work more efficiently.

Birkinshaw & Cohen (2013)

Part 1 · Time management
The theory · Tool 2

Slow Productivity: do fewer things, better

Most workplaces judge effort by how busy people look. Cal Newport, a professor at Georgetown University, calls this pseudo productivity:

“using visible activity as a crude proxy for actual productivity”Newport, in Epstein (2024)

His alternative is slow productivity. Slow does not mean lazy. It means fewer things at the same time, each one done properly. It rests on three principles.

Do fewer thingsFewer commitments at the same time, so the ones that matter get finished.
Work at a natural paceRealistic deadlines, and a quieter stretch planned after a busy one.
Obsess over qualityYour best hours go to what only you can do: strategy and your people.

The overhead tax

“Every commitment that you make brings with it some amount of administrative overhead, such as emails or meetings.”Newport, in Epstein (2024)

Each project comes with its own messages, check ins and follow ups. Add enough projects and the overhead fills the day.

Three limits

Limit missions“One or two main objectives that direct your professional life is ideal; five or more are hard to maintain.”
Limit projectsBefore saying yes, find the time in your calendar. “If you can’t find the time on your calendar, you don’t have the time to do it.”
Limit daily goalsRequests go on a shared list, added by the person asking, with all the details.

Keep a queue, not a pile

Keep two lists: a small number of commitments you are working on now, and a queue of things waiting. New requests join the end of the queue, and everyone can see it.

Newport (2024a, 2024b); Epstein (2024)

Part 1 · Time management
The theory · Tool 3

Book thinking time like a meeting

Strategic thinking needs a long stretch of quiet time. Nobody can plan next year in the ten minutes between two meetings. So put thinking time in the calendar as if it were a meeting with an important client, and do not give it away.

“A single meeting can blow a whole afternoon, by breaking it into two pieces each too small to do anything hard in.”Graham (2009)

Rules that protect the blocks

  • Two strategy blocks a week of two hours each, marked busy, at the time of day when you think best.
  • One development block a week for coaching, KPI reviews and PDP reviews.
  • Messages in batches, at set times.
  • Meetings together, in the same half days.
  • A rule for “just 15 minutes”. Decide in advance what may break a block.

Questions for a strategy block

  • Where should this team be in 6 to 12 months?
  • Which KPI is moving the wrong way, and why?
  • What could go wrong next quarter?
  • What should the team stop doing?
  • Who is ready for more?
  • What one improvement would clients feel most?
Part 1 · Time management
Summary

Part 1 in one page

  • 1Switching between tasks has a price, so a day cut into fragments costs more than its minutes.
  • 2Run every recurring task through three questions, in order: drop, delegate, redesign.
  • 3Do fewer things at once. Find the time in your calendar before you say yes.
  • 4New requests join a queue that everyone can see. They do not land on the pile.
  • 5Book thinking time like a meeting with an important client, and do not give it away.

Part 2 · Essentialism

Essentialism

Less, but better

Part 2 · Essentialism
The theory

Less, but better

Part 1 freed hours. Essentialism asks the harder question: what are those hours for? Greg McKeown’s book is built on one principle from the designer Dieter Rams: “Weniger aber besser”, less but better.

“Essentialism is not about how to get more things done; it’s about how to get the right things done.”McKeown (2014)

Two ways of working

NonessentialistEssentialist
All things to all peopleLess but better
“I have to.” “How can I fit it all in?”“I choose to.” “What are the trade-offs?”
Says “yes” to people without really thinkingSays “no” to everything except the essential
Takes on too much, and work suffersChooses carefully in order to do great work
“If you don’t prioritize your life, someone else will.”McKeown (2014)

Three steps

ExploreWhat really matters? Take time to think before committing.
EliminateWhat can we cut? Say no to good opportunities to protect the best ones.
ExecuteHow do we make the essential easy? Remove obstacles, build buffers, make progress visible.
Part 2 · Essentialism
The theory · Tools

Tools from Essentialism

The 90 Percent RuleScore an option from 0 to 100 on your most important criterion. “If you rate it any lower than 90 percent, then automatically change the rating to 0 and simply reject it.” In short: “If it isn’t a clear yes, then it’s a clear no.”
A zero-based calendarImagine all your commitments are gone, and ask which ones you would add back today. “Every use of time, energy, or resources has to justify itself anew.”
The reverse pilotNot sure whether a report or meeting matters? Stop it quietly and watch who notices.
The graceful no“denying the request is not the same as denying the person.” To a senior leader: “Yes, I’m happy to make this the priority. Which of these other projects should I deprioritize to pay attention to this new project?”
The bufferPeople underestimate how long work takes. “add a 50 percent buffer to the amount of time we estimate it will take”.

Leading as an Essentialist

AreaThe Essentialist leader
Strategy“If we could only do one thing, what would it be?”
EmpowermentFocuses on each team member’s highest role and goal of contribution
CommunicationListens to get to what is essential
AccountabilityChecks in with people in a gentle way to remove obstacles

McKeown (2014)

Part 2 · Essentialism
The theory

Leading through paradox

Essentialism is about choosing. Tim Elmore adds a different point: many leadership choices are not one or the other, but both at once. Uncommon leaders, he writes, “live in the tension of two opposing views”.

  1. Confidence and humility
  2. Vision and blind spots
  3. Visibility and invisibility
  4. Stubborn and open minded
  5. Deeply personal and inherently collective
  6. Teachers and learners
  7. High standards and gracious forgiveness
  8. Timely and timeless

Four of the eight come back today: 3, 2 and 6 in delegation, and 7 in mistakes and feedback.

Watch: Tim Elmore on the 8 paradoxes

Elmore (2021)

Part 2 · Essentialism
Summary

Part 2 in one page

  • 1Strategy time does not come from working faster. It comes from choosing.
  • 2Explore, eliminate, execute: think first, cut the good to protect the best, then make the essential easy.
  • 3If it isn’t a clear yes, it’s a clear no.
  • 4A graceful no separates the decision from the relationship.
  • 5Great leaders hold two opposite qualities at once.

Part 3 · Delegation

Delegation

Let go, stay close

Part 3 · Delegation
The theory

Every task handed over leaves the 70

Delegation is where most of the twenty points come from. It is also the main way people grow. Most managers fail in one of two directions: they never really let go, or they let go and disappear.

Three paradoxes behind good delegation

Paradox 3 · Visibility and invisibilityEarly on, people need to see you do the work: “People do what people see.” Over time, you step aside so they can own it. Elmore’s step: “choose to be absent from meetings so they can step up.”
Paradox 2 · Vision and blind spotsNewer people do not know what “can’t be done”, and that is sometimes what a problem needs. Hand over the problem and let the person choose the method: “‘Marry’ the problem you’re trying to solve but ‘date’ your methods.”
Paradox 6 · Teachers and learnersWhen you delegate, you teach. You also learn, because the person often finds a better way. Uncommon leaders say: “Speak to me and I’ll listen.”

What the research says

1,751%
average three year growth rate of CEOs with high Delegator talent, “112 percentage points greater” than other CEOs. A correlation in one group, but letting go is linked with growth.Badal & Ott (2015), Gallup

A meta-analysis of 105 samples found “positive effects of EL on performance, organizational citizenship behavior, and creativity”. EL means empowering leadership. It works when people trust the leader and feel able to act. Lee, Willis & Tian (2018)

Part 3 · Delegation
The theory

Why managers don’t delegate

Most managers recognise themselves in at least two of these. Naming the reason matters, because each one needs a different fix.

“Nobody does it as well as I do.”Overvaluing your own way. People value what they made themselves far more than it deserves (Norton, Mochon & Ariely, 2012).
“It’s faster to do it myself.”True this week, false over a quarter.
“I don’t want to overload them.”Guilt. Seeing delegation as helping people grow reduces it (Akinola, Martin & Phillips, 2018).
“If it goes wrong, it’s on me.”Fear of risk and blame. The levels below manage exactly this.
“My boss expects me to know every detail.”Pressure from above.
“This work is who I am.”Identity and loss.
“Nobody on my team is ready.”Usually a level problem, not a people problem.
A simple sumA weekly report takes you one hour. Teaching someone else takes three hours, once. The time is paid back in week four, and after that you get more than forty hours a year back. (The numbers are an illustration.)
Part 3 · Delegation
Your turn

Why don’t we delegate at ArpuPlus?

Pick one real task and answer honestly. You will use the same task in the next two exercises.

Part 3 · Delegation
The tool

The Control Check

“I like to be in control. I like things done my way.”

This is the reason managers find hardest to say aloud. It is not a character flaw. It is a thought pattern, and thought patterns can change. This tool is adapted from the thought record used in Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (Beck, 2021). Take the task you named and work through the six steps.

Example: “If I don’t review every line, the client will get a bad report.”

2. Spot the thinking trap. Tick the ones that fit

Example: “Omar will do it differently, and at first it may be less polished. The numbers will be right, which is what the client needs.”

Part 3 · Delegation
The theory

What, to whom, and how much

What to delegate, and what to keep

DelegateKeep
Recurring tasks someone can learnDirection and priorities
Tasks where they know more than youPerformance, pay and development conversations
Tasks that would stretch someoneSensitive people matters
Decisions close to their daily workDecisions too risky for their current readiness

To whom: readiness levels

Readiness is about one task, not one person.

R1 · Enthusiastic beginnerLow skill, high motivation. Telling: clear steps, close checks.
R2 · Disillusioned learnerSome skill, shaken confidence. Selling: explain the why, encourage.
R3 · Capable but cautiousGood skill, hesitant to decide. Collaborating: ask their view.
R4 · Self-reliant achieverHigh skill, high confidence. Delegating: agree the outcome and step back.

Do not judge readiness alone. Research found the model works “when leader rating and follower self-rating are congruent”. Ask the person how ready they feel, and settle the level together. Thompson & Glasø (2018)

How much authority: seven levels

  1. TellI decide and tell you.
  2. SellI decide and explain why.
  3. ConsultI ask your view, then I decide.
  4. AgreeWe decide together.
  5. AdviseI give my view, you decide.
  6. InquireYou decide, then tell me.
  7. DelegateYou decide.

The level belongs to a decision area, not to a person. Say it out loud. The most common failure is a mismatch nobody named: you think level 6, they heard level 3.

Blanchard, Zigarmi & Zigarmi (1985); Appelo (2011)

Part 3 · Delegation
Template

The Delegation Brief

Use the task from the Control Check. Eight questions, answered in a line or two each.

The handover conversation

  1. 1
    Give the context.
  2. 2
    Describe the outcome and the deadline.
  3. 3
    Say the level out loud.
  4. 4
    Agree the limits and the resources.
  5. 5
    Agree the check-ins and the early warning signs.
  6. 6
    Ask them to repeat it back in their own words.
  7. 7
    Ask what they need from you, then step back.

Staying close without taking it back

  • Keep to the agreed check-ins.
  • Ask “what do you suggest?” before giving an answer.
  • Accept a different way of doing it.
  • Raise the level when a task goes well twice.
Part 3 · Delegation
The theory · Paradox 7

High standards and gracious forgiveness

How you respond the first time delegated work goes wrong decides whether the person takes initiative a second time. Most managers think standards and forgiveness pull against each other. Elmore’s point is that each only works with the other.

“When team members know their leader holds high standards, yet is willing to forgive mistakes, it frees them to push themselves, take appropriate risks, and initiate when they might normally hold back and play it safe.”Elmore (2021)
High standards, no forgivenessThe team plays it safe. “They won’t take risks.”
Forgiveness, no high standardsThe team coasts. “Average expectations with an ‘easy out’ lead to mediocrity.”
Both together“Teams do more than they felt possible.”

The safety net

When the Golden Gate Bridge was built, the chief engineer put a safety net under the workers. “The net saved the lives of nineteen falling workers”, and “the work sped up as everyone felt empowered to focus on completing their work rather than on their own safety.” The standards are the height of the bridge. Forgiveness is the net.

What to do

  • “Offer the Gift of Clarity. Make sure the people you lead understand what a ‘win’ looks like.”
  • “Communicate your high expectations but model your forgiveness.”
  • “Extend the Safety Net Principle.”
  • “Practice ‘Try It Out and Talk It Over.’”
Part 3 · Delegation
The theory

When delegated work goes wrong

The blame gap

Amy Edmondson asks executives how many failures are truly blameworthy: “their answers are usually in the single digits”. Asked how many are treated as blameworthy, they say “70 percent to 90 percent”. The result: “many failures go unreported, and their lessons are lost.”

A spectrum of reasons for failure

  1. DevianceSomeone chose to break a rule.
  2. InattentionSomeone drifted from the standard.
  3. Lack of abilityThe person did not have the skill or training.
  4. Process inadequacyThe process itself was faulty.
  5. Task challengeThe task was too hard to do reliably.
  6. Process complexityMany parts interacted in a new way.
  7. UncertaintyA reasonable decision, an unknown future.
  8. Hypothesis testingA test to prove an idea, which failed.
  9. Exploratory testingAn experiment to learn something new.

The list runs from most blameworthy to most praiseworthy. The response should match the reason, not the size of the damage.

The blameless review

  1. 1
    What happened, step by step?
  2. 2
    Why did it make sense to the people involved at the time?
  3. 3
    What in the system allowed it?
  4. 4
    What will we change, and who owns it?

Blameless does not mean consequence free. Honest mistakes inside a reasonable process are not punished. Deliberate rule breaking still gets a firm response.

Edmondson (2011)

Part 3 · Delegation
The theory

How to make sure delegation is done right

Elmore describes moving from “empower by example” to “empower by experience”, with four ingredients he calls the Big IDEA.

InstructionExplain the why as well as the what. “People need conversations.”
DemonstrationShow what good looks like. “People need observation.”
ExperienceLet the person do it on their own. “People need application.”
AssessmentReview it together afterwards. “People need evaluation.”
“I don’t believe experience is the best teacher; I believe experience plus evaluation is the best teacher.”Elmore (2021)

A checklist for every handover

BeforeThe outcome and deadline are written down. The must haves are separated from “my way”. The level is named out loud.
DuringCheck-ins happen when agreed, and the person leads them. They bring a suggestion with every problem.
AfterReview it together. Agree the level for next time. Give the credit to the person, in front of others.
Part 3 · Delegation
Summary

Part 3 in one page

  • 1Name your real reason for not delegating. Each reason needs a different fix.
  • 2Separate the must haves from “my way”. Only the must haves go into the brief.
  • 3Agree readiness with the person, and say the delegation level out loud.
  • 4Hold high standards and offer a safety net. Each only works with the other.
  • 5When it goes wrong, ask why it made sense at the time before deciding what went wrong.

Part 4 · KPIs and feedback

KPIs and feedback

How to set them, and the feedback that makes them work

Part 4 · KPIs and feedback
The theory

A steering tool before a reporting tool

A KPI (Key Performance Indicator) is a number that shows whether the most important results of a role are being achieved. It is a steering tool for the employee before it is a reporting tool for the manager. Clear KPIs are what make delegation safe.

WordMeaning and example
GoalThe result we want. Onboard new partners faster.
MetricAnything we can count. Number of integrations started.
KPIThe few metrics that show the goal is being met. Share of integrations live within 10 working days.
TargetThe level we aim for, by a date. 8 out of 10 by 30 June.

What the research says

“what you measure is what you get”Kaplan & Norton (1992)
.42 to .80
Specific goals beat “do your best”. “The effect sizes in meta-analyses ranged from .42 to .80”. Goals work best when people are committed to them and get feedback on progress.Locke & Latham (2002)
4×
Employees whose manager involves them in goal setting “are four times more likely to be engaged than other employees.”Gallup
“When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.”Strathern (1997)

The lesson is not to avoid targets. It is to design KPIs that are hard to game.

Part 4 · KPIs and feedback
The theory

How to set KPIs

The anatomy of a good KPI

  1. 1
    An outcome, not an activity.
  2. 2
    A clear formula and data source. Two people get the same number.
  3. 3
    A baseline, and a target with a date.
  4. 4
    A leading indicator. An early signal.
  5. 5
    A guardrail. A second measure that protects quality.

Seven steps

  1. 1
    Start from the team goal. Why does this matter to ArpuPlus?
  2. 2
    Name the key results of the role. “If this person did the job brilliantly for six months, what would be different?”
  3. 3
    Choose the measure: quantity, quality, time, cost or satisfaction.
  4. 4
    Define it so two people get the same number.
  5. 5
    Set the baseline, then the target and the date.
  6. 6
    Add a leading indicator and a guardrail.
  7. 7
    Agree it with the employee, and set the review rhythm.

Three KPIs per person is enough, five at most. SMART is a useful check on the wording, but it is a checklist, not a theory (Doran, 1981; Swann et al., 2023).

Weak and strong KPIs

WeakStrong
Handle partner integrations8 out of 10 new integrations live within 10 working days by 30 June, with no critical defect in the first 30 days
Close 40 tickets a week90% of tickets resolved at first contact, with client rating of 4 out of 5 or more
Make 30 client calls a weekRenewal rate of 85% this year, with average discount under 10%

Three tests before agreeing a KPI

The Monday testWould this person know what to do differently on Monday morning?
The gaming testHow could someone hit this number and hurt the business? Does the guardrail stop it?
The line of sight testCan the person explain how this KPI helps the team goal, without my help?

For work that is new to the person, set a learning goal first, such as “find three ways to cut onboarding time by the end of the month” (Seijts & Latham, 2005).

Part 4 · KPIs and feedback
The theory

Feedback: what makes a KPI move

A KPI on its own changes nothing. People also need regular feedback on their progress. But feedback is not automatically helpful.

Back to Paradox 7

The KPI is the high standard. The way you give feedback is the safety net.

High standardsGracious forgiveness
Name the gap against the KPI plainly.Keep it about the work, not the person.
Agree what good looks like next time.Treat the miss as information, not a verdict.
Follow up at the next review.Ask what got in the way before deciding what went wrong.
1 in 3
“FIs improved performance on average (d=.41) but that over 1/3 of the FIs decreased performance.” FI means feedback intervention.Kluger & DeNisi (1996)

Keep it on the task

Feedback aimed atExample and effect
The self“You are careless.” Least effective.
Motivation“This matters for the client renewal.” In between.
The task“Two totals in the billing file don’t match the source.” Most effective.

Look forward, not back

A study of feedback conversations found that “Disagreement regarding past performance was greater following the feedback discussion than before”. What predicted motivation to improve was a conversation “focused on future actions”. Spend one minute on what happened and the rest on what to do next. Gnepp et al. (2020)

Part 4 · KPIs and feedback
The tool

SBI, plus a next step

SituationWhen and where. “In this morning’s partner call…”
BehaviourWhat a camera would have recorded. “…you answered before the client finished explaining the outage…”
ImpactWhat it caused. “…so they stopped giving details we needed.”
Next stepThe future, ending with a question. “Next call, let them finish, then summarise. What would help?”

Now write one piece of feedback you need to give this week.

The KPI review conversation

  1. 1
    Look at the number together.
  2. 2
    Ask them to read it first: “what do you see?”
  3. 3
    Give SBI feedback on what helped or hurt.
  4. 4
    Agree one action.
  5. 5
    Check the KPI still measures the right thing.

SBI from the Center for Creative Leadership; next step added for this program

Part 4 · KPIs and feedback
Summary

Part 4 in one page

  • 1A good KPI measures an outcome, has a formula, a baseline, a target with a date, a leading indicator and a guardrail.
  • 2Set KPIs with people, not for them. Three per person is enough.
  • 3Test every KPI: Monday, gaming, line of sight.
  • 4Feedback works when it stays on the task and looks forward.
  • 5Situation, Behaviour, Impact, Next step.

Part 5 · Coaching with GROW

Coaching with GROW

Help people think for themselves

Part 5 · Coaching with GROW
The theory

Ask before you tell

Coaching means helping someone think their way to their own answer, instead of giving them yours. It is slower than telling in the first conversation and much faster over a year, because the person stops coming back with the same kind of question.

“The best coach for an employee is their manager.”Gallup (2019)

A meta-analysis found that “coaching had positive effects on organizational outcomes overall”, “with effects being stronger for internal coaches compared to external coaches”. Jones, Woods & Guillaume (2016)

The GROW model

GoalWhat do you want to achieve? What would success look like?
RealityWhat is happening now? What have you tried? What is getting in the way?
OptionsWhat could you do? What else? Who could help?
WillWhat will you do? By when? What do you need from me?

The coach asks. The coachee answers. The coachee owns the plan.

How to run a GROW conversation

  1. 1
    Start with their goal, not your agenda.
  2. 2
    Stay in Reality long enough.
  3. 3
    Ask “what else?” at least twice in Options.
  4. 4
    Hold back your own idea.
  5. 5
    End with Will: a specific action and a date.
  6. 6
    Follow up at the next one to one.

When to coach, and when not to

SituationBetter approach
They have the skill but hesitate (R3)Coach
They are skilled and confident (R4)Coach lightly, mostly listen
They are new to the task (R1)Tell and show first, coach later
A real emergencyDecide now, review together afterwards

GROW as set out in Whitmore (2017)

Part 5 · Coaching with GROW
Summary

Part 5 in one page

  • 1Coaching is slower today and faster over a year.
  • 2Goal, Reality, Options, Will.
  • 3Good Reality questions do half the work.
  • 4The biggest trap is jumping from Reality to your own solution.
  • 5No date, no commitment.

Part 6 · PDPs

PDPs

How to create one for an employee

Part 6 · PDPs
The theory

A one page plan the employee owns

A Personal Development Plan (PDP) is a one page plan for how a person will grow over the next 6 to 12 months. The employee owns it and writes it. The manager coaches it out of them and commits to the support.

KPIPDP
What results does this role need to deliver?How will this person grow?
Performance nowCapability for the future
A number, a target and a dateA capability, actions and review dates

What the research says

44%
higher retention, and 16% higher productivity, when the share of employees with opportunities to learn and grow doubles. These are modelled estimates.Gallup (2019)

A PDP only works when it is supported. A study of 287 employees looked at “three supporting conditions: learning and reflection, information and feedback and the motivating supervisor”. Beausaert, Segers & Gijselaers (2011)

Most development happens on the job: “70% challenging experiences and assignments”, “20% developmental relationships” and “10% coursework and training”. In this program we call them experience, people and learning. Center for Creative Leadership (2025)

Part 6 · PDPs
The theory

How to create a PDP

  1. 1
    Prepare, both of you. Send three questions a few days before: What do you enjoy most? What do you want to be able to do in a year? Where do you want to be in two years?
  2. 2
    Hold the conversation with GROW. You ask, they answer and write.
  3. 3
    Choose one or two development goals. Write each as a capability with a date: “Lead partner calls on my own by June”.
  4. 4
    Choose the actions: experience, people, learning. Most of the plan should be experience.
  5. 5
    Agree your support and how you will know.
  6. 6
    Set the review dates and keep them: 30 days, 90 days, then every quarter.

Three kinds of action

ExperienceReal work that stretches the person. A delegated task at a rising delegation level.
PeopleLearning from others. Shadowing, a mentor, feedback after key moments.
LearningFormal study. A short course, a certification, a book.

A worked example

Omar is a Partner Integration Specialist, one year into the job. (The example is fictional.)

SectionOmar’s plan
GoalLead partner calls with confidence: from R1 to R3 by June
ExperienceOwn one delegated integration, with the level rising from 2 to 5
PeopleShadow Laila on two client calls
LearningOne short course on client communication
Manager’s supportWeekly 15 minute check in; join the first two calls, then step back
Review30 days, 90 days, then each quarter

Weak and strong development goals

WeakStrong
Improve communication skillsPresent the monthly partner review to the client on my own by April
Attend a management courseCoach one junior colleague through their first integration, using GROW, by June

The PDP template

Part 6 · PDPs
Summary

Part 6 in one page

  • 1The employee owns the PDP. The manager coaches it out of them.
  • 2One or two development goals, written as capabilities with dates.
  • 3Most of the plan is real work: the task you delegate becomes the main action.
  • 4Your support goes on the page.
  • 5A PDP with no review date is a wish list.
